marks: Chinese chronicles of the 4th century BCE record Tengri as the sky god of the Xiongnu.
The Old Turkic inscriptions of the Orkhon say that the khagans acted because “Heaven so ordained”.
William of Rubruck heard Ariq Böke, Hulegu’s brother, say near Karakorum in 1254: “we know that the Messiah is God”.
Hulegu Khan wrote from his capital here to Louis IX of France in 1262, in a letter that calls Christ “Messiah-Tengri”.
Arghun wrote here in 1290 to Pope Nicholas IV that prayer to Eternal Tengri with righteous thoughts was as much as baptism.
Seat of the International Fund of Tengri Research; the Tengrist organisation Kut-Siur was founded in Sakha in 1990–1993.
Askar Akayev called his visit to the Yenisei inscriptions here in 2002 “like a pilgrimage to a holy place for the Kyrgyz people”.
Tengir Ordo held the first international scientific symposium on Tengrism here in 2003.
notes: Chinese chronicles record Tengri, the sky god of the Xiongnu, in the 4th century BCE.
The Xiongnu empire is founded (209 BCE), first of a line of steppe khanates and empires whose faith is Tengrism.
The Göktürk khaganates record in the Orkhon inscriptions that their khagans rule because “Heaven so ordained”.
The Irk Bitig, a 9th-century book of divination from the Uyghur Khaganate, calls Tengri the god of the Turks; the Magyars keep a form of Tengrism until the end of the 10th century.
Genghis Khan’s successors are Tengrist “shaman-kings”; the Secret History of the Mongols (1240) and the letters of Hulegu (1262) and Arghun (1290) invoke the power of Eternal Tengri.
Özbeg Khan of the Golden Horde turns to Islam, and the Turkic and Mongolic peoples of Central Asia largely convert during the 14th century; Tengrism is mostly submerged.
In Mongolia Tengrist formulas are absorbed into Buddhism; the 17th-century chronicle Altan Tobchi ends with a Tengrist prayer, and purer forms survive around Lake Khövsgöl and Lake Baikal.
Kalmyk regiments carry the banner of the war god Daichin Tengri through the Napoleonic Wars to Paris (1814).
Turanism and Kemalism encourage a Tengrist revival in Turkey after 1923; after the dissolution of the Soviet Union (1991) Tengrism is revived in Central Asia, Russia and Siberia.
Tengir Ordo is founded in Kyrgyzstan (2005); over one million people follow Tengrism in Kazakhstan (2024), where it is not officially recognised.
src: The Secret History of the Mongols (1240)
